title: Don't Trash That Pumpkin: Give It a Second Life
summary:
Every fall, tens of millions of pumpkins appear on porches across the United States. Some become jack-o'-lanterns. Others are just decorations. After Halloween, most people think the pumpkin's job is done.

But throwing them away has a big hidden cost. Experts estimate over one billion pounds end up in United States landfills each year, more than 80 percent of the 1.3 billion pounds bought. In the United Kingdom, about 55 percent of 39 million pumpkins bought go uneaten, worth about $37 million.

When pumpkins rot in landfills, they release methane, a gas that traps much more heat than carbon dioxide over a shorter time. So a simple decoration can add to climate change.

Luckily, there is an easy fix. Roast the seeds for a snack, or turn the flesh into soup, puree, or pie. Donate pumpkins to farms or zoos for animal feed. If one is too old to eat or donate, bury it in your yard to feed the soil. That small choice, across millions of homes, can cut waste and help our environment.
why_it_matters: After Halloween, you can turn your own pumpkin into a snack or soup, or bury it to feed the soil, instead of letting it add to climate-changing waste.

background_read: A pumpkin is a big orange fruit that grows on a vine in the fall and is often carved into a jack-o'-lantern or used as a decoration for Halloween.
When food is thrown away, it goes to a landfill, a place where trash is buried, and as it rots there it can release methane, a gas that traps heat and adds to climate change.
That is why people look for other uses for old pumpkins, such as cooking them, feeding them to animals, or burying them in soil where they can break down and feed plants.
